units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero-aligned record and explains the interval error.
units.task: Two fictional ruler records measure the same strip. One begins at zero and the other at the ruler edge before zero. Identify which record is defensible and explain the role of the zero mark.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can define gravity as a downward pull from the Earth.
units.task: Drop various objects (a ball, a crumpled paper, a pencil) to demonstrate that they all fall downwards. Explicitly teach that gravity is the Earth's downward pull.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can define a force as a push or a pull that changes motion.
units.task: Introduce forces as pushes and pulls using a toy car. Demonstrate pushing to start, pulling to move closer, and pushing/pulling to stop the car.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can describe the two directions of movement in projectile motion.
units.task: Demonstrate projectile motion by tossing a ball into a bin. Discuss how the ball moves forward and up/down at the same time.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain why the broken ruler gives a false reading.
units.task: Present a ruler with the first 2 cm snapped off. Demonstrate how measuring a 5 cm object with it gives an incorrect reading if not adjusted, explaining reliability.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can identify a thermometer and state its purpose.
units.task: Introduce the thermometer as an instrument for measuring temperature. Show different types (clinical, environmental) and discuss their uses.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly states the unit used for mass, volume, and length when prompted.
units.task: Introduce standard units (g, L, cm) by displaying common household items and explicitly teaching which unit corresponds to mass, volume, and length.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally explain the importance of starting at the zero mark.
units.task: Demonstrate how to align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object and read the measurement in centimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point out the poles as the areas with the most iron filings.
units.task: Demonstrate placing a piece of paper over a bar magnet and sprinkling iron filings to reveal the magnetic field lines, explaining the concentration at the poles.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can articulate that different scales have different sensitivities.
units.task: Show a bathroom scale and a kitchen scale. Place a spoonful of salt on both to demonstrate that the bathroom scale does not register the small mass.

units.mastery_criterion: Students state that melting is reversible because water can be frozen again, while cutting an apple is irreversible.
units.task: Observe the teacher melt an ice cube and then show a pre-frozen ice cube. Then observe the teacher cut an apple. Discuss which change can be undone.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the colored water as homogeneous and the sandy water as heterogeneous.
units.task: Mix water with food coloring in one clear cup, and water with sand in another. Discuss which mixture looks the same throughout and which does not.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify tearing as physical and mixing as chemical, citing the formation of bubbles as evidence of a new substance.
units.task: Observe teacher tear paper and mix baking soda with vinegar. Discuss and classify each change as physical or chemical based on whether a new substance is formed.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct rock type when the teacher describes a key feature (e.g., 'has fossils' -> sedimentary).
units.task: Introduce igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks using large physical samples or high-quality images. Highlight key observable features (crystals, layers/fossils, banding).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can name the three compositional layers and state that physical properties like density differences keep them from mixing.
units.task: Cut a hard-boiled egg in half to model the Earth's compositional layers (shell=crust, white=mantle, yolk=core). Explain that real layers separate due to different physical properties like density, distinguishing between the names of the layers and the reason they separate.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally define simple and compound substances based on the block models.
units.task: Use colored interlocking blocks to demonstrate simple substances (all blocks same color) and compound substances (blocks of different colors joined together).

units.mastery_criterion: Students articulate that the candle went out because it used up the oxygen, and connect this to human need for atmospheric oxygen.
units.task: Teacher lights a small candle and covers it with a glass jar. Students observe it go out. Discuss that fire needs oxygen from the air, just like humans do.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that fluid lava creates wide, flat shapes (shield) and thick lava creates steep shapes (stratovolcano).
units.task: Pour water (fluid lava model) and thick syrup (viscous lava model) onto a flat tray. Observe how they spread or pile up. Discuss how this relates to volcano shapes.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally repeat the sequence of processes that turn a surface rock into magma.
units.task: Introduce the rock cycle using a large wall diagram. Explain weathering, erosion, deformation, and melting as the processes that move rocks through the cycle.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can define soluble as dissolving in water and insoluble as not dissolving.
units.task: Demonstrate mixing salt in water (soluble) and sand in water (insoluble). Define the terms soluble and insoluble.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally name at least three water bodies shown in the photographs.
units.task: Observe photographs of oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, and aquifers. Discuss the defining characteristics of each water body.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point to the aquifer on the diagram and explain how water got there.
units.task: Show a diagram of soil layers and explain how rain soaks into the ground to form aquifers.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state two negative effects of lack of water on living things.
units.task: Discuss the biological need for water in plants and animals, and introduce the concept of drought.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally list the three main stages of human water use.
units.task: Explain the cycle of extracting water from the environment, using it in homes, and discharging wastewater.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the root system (below ground) and shoot system (above ground) with their respective organs.
units.task: Students observe a complete uprooted weed (provided by the teacher), draw it, and label the shoot and root systems, listing the organs found in each.

units.mastery_criterion: Written definition includes 'slow', 'directional', and 'growth response'.
units.task: Students watch a time-lapse video of a plant growing towards light, then write a definition of tropism and explain why time-lapse is needed to see it.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can define a vertebrate as an animal with a backbone.
units.task: Introduce the concept of vertebrates having a backbone and invertebrates lacking one using models.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state whether moving toward a stimulus is positive or negative.
units.task: Define positive and negative taxism with examples like a moth to light and a worm away from light.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that gills extract oxygen from water and lungs from air, and use this to infer habitat.
units.task: Discuss the differences between gills and lungs, focusing on oxygen extraction in water versus air, and model how to deduce an animal's habitat based on its respiratory organs.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly points to the central axis or lack thereof when asked.
units.task: Introduce bilateral, radial, and asymmetrical body plans using large printed photos of a butterfly, sea star, and sponge.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally link one structure to its specific feeding function.
units.task: Show pictures of beaks, tongues, and tentacles, explaining how each is used for feeding.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally define metamorphosis and name the four stages in order when prompted.
units.task: Explain the mosquito life cycle using a step-by-step diagram on the board, explicitly defining 'metamorphosis' as the process encompassing these developmental stages.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly points to and names the nucleus as the defining feature of a eukaryotic cell.
units.task: Present large diagrams of a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell. Guide students to identify the nucleus in the eukaryotic cell and note its absence in the prokaryotic cell. Students trace the nucleus with a marker on their own copies.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can list moisture and warm temperatures as optimal conditions for microbial growth.
units.task: Introduce the optimal conditions for microbial growth: moisture, warm temperatures, and oxygen. Use photos of fresh bread versus moldy bread to explain how these conditions accelerate decomposition.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state one characteristic of fungi and one of protozoa.
units.task: Introduce fungi and protozoa. Explain that fungi grow from spores on food, and protozoa live in water and hunt bacteria. Show pictures of mold on bread and a paramecium.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can list metabolism and independent reproduction as key traits of living organisms.
units.task: Introduce the characteristics of living organisms, focusing on metabolism and independent reproduction. Use a chart to compare living organisms with non-living things.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can name encurtido and dried fish as local preservation methods.
units.task: Discuss local Salvadoran preservation methods. Show examples or pictures of 'encurtido' (pickled vegetables) and 'pescado seco' (dried fish). Explain how salt, vinegar, and sun-drying keep food from spoiling.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can identify and describe the protective covers of pathogens.
units.task: Explain the structure of pathogens, specifically focusing on their protective covers like cell walls and capsules. Show diagrams of different pathogens highlighting these layers.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that bleach destroys microorganisms in water and name one household method.
units.task: Survey students about common household water purification methods used in their homes. Discuss the dangers of microorganisms in stagnant water and explain how specific chemicals, like household bleach (lejia), act as disinfectants to destroy these microorganisms.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that equilibrium means forces and torque are balanced and cancel each other out.
units.task: Demonstrate balancing a ruler on a fulcrum. Explain that gravity pulls down, but the fulcrum pushes up, and introduce torque as the rotational force that must be balanced for rotational equilibrium.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that friction opposes motion and makes objects stop faster on rougher surfaces.
units.task: Slide a book across a smooth table and then across a piece of carpet. Ask students to predict and observe the difference. Explicitly teach that friction is the force opposing the motion, causing it to stop faster on rough surfaces.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that objects with more mass require more force to move.
units.task: Demonstrate pushing an empty cardboard box versus a box filled with heavy books across the floor. Introduce the dynamometer as a tool to measure the force applied. Discuss why the heavier box requires more effort.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the magnet was used because clips are magnetic, and the filter was used because sand particles are larger than water particles.
units.task: Demonstrate using a magnet to separate iron clips from sand, and a paper filter to separate sand from water. Discuss why each tool was chosen based on material properties.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can name the three types of mixtures shown.
units.task: Show a solution (saltwater), a colloid (milk in water), and a suspension (dirt in water). Shine a flashlight through each to show light scattering and settling.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that more drops make the water a darker color.
units.task: Add 1, 3, and 6 drops of food coloring to three identical cups of water. Discuss how the color intensity relates to the amount of coloring added.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that most of Earths water is salt water.
units.task: Introduce the concept of Earths water distribution using a 100-part grid to represent total water.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that water moves from higher to lower ground.
units.task: Demonstrate how water flows downhill by pouring water over a slanted plastic board into a basin.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort 100% of the description cards into the transpiration or photosynthesis categories.
units.task: Students review diagrams of a leaf showing water leaving (transpiration) and sunlight/air entering to make food (photosynthesis), then complete a sorting activity with cards describing each process.

units.mastery_criterion: Students consistently draw wide shapes for fluid lava prompts and steep shapes for thick lava prompts.
units.task: Quick draw: Teacher reads an eruption scenario. Students have 2 minutes to draw the resulting volcano shape on a whiteboard and hold it up.

units.mastery_criterion: Student writes down moisture (water/wetness) and warmth (temperature).
units.task: Provide a single image of a rotting fruit. Ask students to write down the two environmental conditions that most likely caused it to rot quickly.

units.mastery_criterion: Student justifies that microorganisms are invisible and require purification methods like bleach to be destroyed.
units.task: Students evaluate a false claim: 'Clear water is always safe to drink.' They write a paragraph justifying why this is false, referencing invisible microorganisms and the need for purification.

units.mastery_criterion: Chart accurately lists water absorption for roots, water transport for stems, and support functions for both.
units.task: Students examine cross-sections of stems and roots using hand lenses, then create a two-column chart detailing the transport and support functions of each.

units.mastery_criterion: Sequence map correctly shows the progression from flower to fruit to seed.
units.task: Students dissect a large flower (like a lily) and a soft fruit (like a tomato) to locate reproductive parts and seeds, recording their findings in a sequence map from flower to fruit.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify gravitropism, phototropism, hydrotropism, and thigmotropism at the stations.
units.task: Students rotate through four stations showing images/models of different tropisms (roots down, stem to light, roots to water, vine on fence) and record the specific tropism name for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Definition includes 'fast' and 'non-directional response'.
units.task: Students observe a video of a Venus flytrap and a Mimosa pudica closing, then write a definition of nastia focusing on speed and lack of directional growth.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can name one key trait for mollusks, arthropods, and worms.
units.task: Introduce major invertebrate groups (mollusks, arthropods, worms) focusing on key morphological traits.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state the skin covering for mammals and birds.
units.task: Introduce mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish based on skin covering and reproduction.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that salt removes water from food, preventing microbial growth.
units.task: Explain dehydration as a preservation method. Describe how adding salt to food draws out the water, and since microorganisms need water to survive, the food is preserved.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that good bacteria make acid to keep bad bacteria away.
units.task: Introduce the concept of 'good' bacteria. Explain how in foods like cheese or yogurt, beneficial microorganisms produce acid that creates a toxic environment for 'bad' (pathogenic) bacteria, preserving the food.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that cold temperatures slow down microbial growth rather than killing the microbes.
units.task: Explain how refrigeration works to preserve food. Emphasize that cold temperatures do not kill microorganisms, but rather slow down their growth and reproduction.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally list at least two reasons why a virus is not considered a standard living organism.
units.task: Explain the characteristics of viruses using a comparison chart on the board. Emphasize that viruses lack cells, lack metabolism, and need a host to reproduce, which makes them different from living organisms.

units.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
units.task: Demonstrate the action of soap using a jar with water and oil. Shake it to show they separate. Add liquid soap and shake again to show them mixing. Compare the two mixtures and state that this is an oil model, not a pathogen-killing test. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can describe the steps of decantation verbally.
units.task: Demonstrate how to separate sand and water by letting the sand settle and carefully pouring the water into a new cup.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can identify the cotton as the filter that catches the solid particles.
units.task: Use a fictional Salvadoran community water-supply diagram and teacher-prepared water containing clean sand. Apply the supplied filtration procedure to remove visible suspended particles. Explain that clear filtered water is not necessarily safe to drink; no sample is tasted.

units.mastery_criterion: Matrix correctly identifies ferns as using spores, pines as using cones/naked seeds, and flowering plants as using fruits/seeds.
units.task: Students examine fern fronds with spores and pine cones, comparing them to a flowering plant, and fill out a classification matrix based on reproductive structures.

units.mastery_criterion: Justifications correctly reference the speed (slow vs fast) and directionality (directional vs non-directional) of the movement.
units.task: Students are given cards with descriptions of various plant movements and must sort them into 'Tropism' or 'Nastia', writing a justification for each based on speed and direction.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point to the correct next step on the key when asked.
units.task: Walk through a simple 3-step dichotomous key on the board to identify a common animal.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain why decantation should happen before filtration.
units.task: Discuss how decantation and filtration can be combined to clean very dirty water, explaining why settling heavy items first makes filtering easier.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state one anatomical reason why a whale is a mammal.
units.task: Model how to justify classification using anatomical evidence, explaining why a whale is a mammal.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the directional growth of the stem toward the light and identify it as phototropism.
units.task: Students design a simple maze inside a cardboard box for a bean sprout to grow through towards a light hole, recording its phototropic response over a week.

units.mastery_criterion: Students record accurate observations of water moving up the stem and reason that roots would have absorbed the water first.
units.task: Students place celery stalks in colored water and observe them over two days, recording the height of the color in the stem and predicting what would happen if the roots were still attached.

units.mastery_criterion: Student provides at least two anatomical reasons for classifying the animal as a mammal.
units.task: A dolphin lives in the ocean, but it has hair, breathes air, and gives birth. Justify why it is a mammal.

units.mastery_criterion: Student provides at least two anatomical reasons for each animal's classification.
units.task: Write justifications for classifying 3 tricky local animals (cusuco/armadillo, manatee, local bat) based on anatomy.

units.mastery_criterion: Student contributes at least one anatomical fact (e.g., backbone, scales) to the discussion.
units.task: Discuss in small groups why a snake is classified as a reptile and not a worm, using anatomical evidence.

units.mastery_criterion: Student justifies why a specific respiratory structure is suited for water or air.
units.task: Read a description of an unknown animal with gills. Deduce its habitat (aquatic) and justify why it cannot survive on land using evidence about oxygen concentration.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly deduces the habitat for all three animals and provides a valid anatomical reason.
units.task: Analyze profiles of three unknown animals with different respiratory structures (gills, lungs, skin) and deduce their habitats, justifying the choice.

units.mastery_criterion: Student includes the fact that gills are adapted for extracting dissolved oxygen from water in their explanation.
units.task: Write a short paragraph deducing the habitat of a newly discovered organism with gills, justifying why it must live in water using evidence about oxygen.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the cell as prokaryotic and justifies the decision by stating the nucleus is missing.
units.task: Students analyze a 'mystery cell' diagram that has many complex structures but no nucleus. They must decide if it is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and write a justification based on evidence.

units.mastery_criterion: Student matches the humid jungle to the fastest decomposition, justifying it with the presence of moisture and warmth.
units.task: Students are given descriptions of three climates (dry desert, humid jungle, cold tundra). They must match the climate to the expected speed of food decomposition and justify their choice.

units.mastery_criterion: Student predicts the maize in the damp shed will spoil first because microbes need moisture to grow.
units.task: Students evaluate a scenario where harvested maize is stored in a damp shed versus a dry silo. They predict which batch will spoil first and justify using evidence about microbial needs.

units.mastery_criterion: Student predicts the salted fish will last longer because the salt removes the water, and microorganisms need water to survive.
units.task: Show a picture of fresh fish and a picture of fish covered in thick salt. Ask the student to predict which will last longer without rotting and explain why using the word 'water' or 'moisture'.

units.mastery_criterion: Student explains that the salt removed the moisture, making it impossible for decomposing microorganisms to survive.
units.task: Students compare photos of fresh meat and heavily salted dried meat. They write a paragraph explaining why the salted meat can be stored at room temperature without rotting.

units.mastery_criterion: Student corrects the statement by explaining that salt preserves food by removing water (dehydration), not by freezing.
units.task: Students evaluate a misconception: 'Salt preserves food by freezing it.' They must write a correction explaining the true mechanism of salt preservation.

units.mastery_criterion: The comic and caption accurately depict good bacteria producing a substance (acid) that is toxic to pathogens.
units.task: Students write a short comic strip where a 'good bacteria' defends a piece of cheese from a 'bad bacteria' by producing acid. They must include a caption explaining the science.

units.mastery_criterion: Student explains that yogurt contains beneficial microbes that create an environment toxic to spoilage microbes.
units.task: Students compare a glass of fresh milk and a cup of yogurt. They write a paragraph explaining why the yogurt lasts longer in the fridge than the fresh milk, referencing the role of beneficial microorganisms.

units.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
units.task: Provide a matching worksheet where students match the substance (Water alone, Water with Soap) to its effect on an oily pathogen (Slides off, Breaks the oily layer apart). Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

units.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
units.task: Students draw a three-step comic strip showing what happens to an 'oily pathogen' when washed with only water versus when washed with water and soap. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

units.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
units.task: Students conduct a safe experiment by placing a drop of oil on a plastic plate, rinsing it with just water, and then scrubbing it with a soapy sponge to observe the difference. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

units.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
units.task: Students sequence a set of 4 cards showing the process of soap molecules attaching to oil and water, and write a short paragraph explaining why washing hands without soap is ineffective against viruses. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states it prevents spoiling and clarifies that cold slows down microbial proliferation, not kills them.
units.task: Ask the student: 'Why do we put milk in the refrigerator instead of leaving it on the table? Does the cold kill the bacteria or just slow them down?'

units.mastery_criterion: The letter explains that warm temperatures allow bacteria to reproduce quickly, while the fridge slows them down.
units.task: Students write a short letter to a friend explaining why they shouldn't leave milk out on the counter all day, specifically mentioning what happens to the bacteria in warm versus cold temperatures.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the 'kills all bacteria' statement as false and rewrites it to state that the fridge slows down bacteria.
units.task: Students evaluate a set of True/False statements about refrigeration (e.g., 'The fridge kills all bacteria'). They must rewrite the false statements to make them true.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects bleach (lejia) and justifies that it acts as a disinfectant that destroys or stops the growth of microorganisms.
units.task: Present a scenario where a family needs to clean stagnant water. Provide options: add sugar, add bleach (lejia), or just let it sit in the sun. Ask the student to choose the best option and write one sentence justifying why.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the bleach scenario as correct and explains that sugar/salt do not act as disinfectants.
units.task: Students read three short scenarios about families trying to clean water. They must identify which family used the correct method (bleach) and explain why the other methods (sugar, salt) failed to destroy microorganisms.

units.mastery_criterion: Poster includes the concept that settling dirt does not remove invisible microorganisms, but bleach destroys them.
units.task: Students are given a hypothetical problem: a community water tank is contaminated. They must design a poster explaining to the community why adding bleach (in correct proportions) is necessary, rather than just letting the dirt settle.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects the heavier box and explicitly links the required force to the object's mass.
units.task: Students read a scenario about an empty box and a box full of books, predict which requires more force to push, and explain why.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states it is unreliable and links the missing starting point to incorrect measurements.
units.task: Students look at a picture of a ruler missing the zero mark and write whether it is reliable for measuring, explaining why.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects kitchen scale and states the bathroom scale is not sensitive enough for small masses.
units.task: Students write a short paragraph choosing whether to use a bathroom scale or a kitchen scale to measure a spoonful of salt, explaining their reasoning.

units.mastery_criterion: Student concludes that the rubber band stretches more (more force) for the object with more mass.
units.task: Students use a rubber band or a simple dynamometer to pull different objects (a wooden block, a block with weights) and observe the force required, relating it to mass.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies damaged tools as unreliable and links the damage to inaccurate readings.
units.task: Students inspect a 'toolkit' of various measuring devices (some intact, some intentionally damaged like a stretched measuring tape) and categorize them as reliable or unreliable, writing a reason for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts items and provides a valid reason based on the object's mass.
units.task: Students are given cards with pictures of various items (e.g., a single coffee bean, a sack of basic grains like beans or rice) and must sort them by which scale is appropriate, justifying their choice.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the heavier object in all pairs.
units.task: Students are shown pairs of objects (e.g., empty backpack vs full backpack) and must quickly point to the one that requires more force to lift.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies it as unreliable because the missing part prevents accurate mass measurement.
units.task: Quick recall: Show an image of a kitchen scale with a missing weighing pan. Ask students to write down if it is reliable and why.

units.mastery_criterion: Student holds up the correct card for at least 8 out of 10 objects.
units.task: Teacher calls out an object (e.g., a feather, a person, a bag of rice) and students hold up a card indicating 'Kitchen Scale' or 'Bathroom Scale'.

units.mastery_criterion: Explains that exhaust gases displace oxygen, and justifies that humans require the oxygen in the atmosphere to breathe and live.
units.task: Explain in writing why a town in a valley with poor air circulation and a buildup of exhaust gases is dangerous for residents, relating it to the human need for atmospheric oxygen.

units.mastery_criterion: Paragraph justifies the spacesuit by stating the Moon lacks an atmosphere with oxygen, which humans need to survive.
units.task: Analyze a scenario of an astronaut on the Moon versus a person on Earth. Write a paragraph justifying why the astronaut needs a spacesuit using knowledge of the atmosphere.

units.mastery_criterion: Students justify that the sealed plant died because it ran out of necessary gases from the atmosphere, showing the atmosphere's importance for life.
units.task: Review time-lapse photos of a plant in a sealed jar versus an open jar. Discuss and write about why the sealed plant died, relating it to atmospheric gases.

units.mastery_criterion: Selects a sieve and justifies the choice by stating that salt particles are much smaller than beans.
units.task: Given a written scenario of a mixture of dry beans and salt, select a separation method and write a justification based on the properties of the materials.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully separate the mixture using a magnet first, then a sieve, justifying choices based on magnetism and size.
units.task: Provide groups with a mixture of gravel, sand, and iron clips. Students must select tools and sequence their actions to separate all three components, justifying their choices.

units.mastery_criterion: Students select a magnet for caps, a sieve or hand-picking for leaves, and a filter for dirt, justifying based on properties.
units.task: Design a theoretical plan to clean a sample of dirty water containing leaves, dirt, and metal bottle caps. Select separation methods and justify them.

units.mastery_criterion: Students quickly and accurately select the correct tool and state the relevant physical property.
units.task: Flashcard game: Teacher shows a mixture (e.g., water and pebbles), students hold up a card showing the best separation tool (filter, magnet, sieve) and explain why.

units.mastery_criterion: Students select the sieve, justifying that size is the differing property, and successfully separate the beads.
units.task: Quick lab: Students are given a mixture of large wooden beads and small plastic beads. They must choose between a magnet, a sieve, or a filter to separate them and do it.

units.mastery_criterion: Predicts stratovolcano and justifies that thick lava and ash pile up steeply rather than spreading out.
units.task: Read data about a volcano that historically erupted with thick, slow-moving lava and large ash clouds. Predict its shape (shield or stratovolcano) and write a justification.

units.mastery_criterion: Students build a wide, flat model for the effusive description and a steep, cone model for the explosive description.
units.task: Students read descriptions of two historical eruptions (one effusive, one explosive) and build clay models of the predicted volcano shapes.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly predicts structures based on eruption images and justifies using the relationship between eruption type and shape.
units.task: Analyze images of different volcanic eruptions (effusive and explosive) from the provided text. Predict the resulting volcano structure for each and justify based on the eruption type.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match fluid/few gases to shield, and thick/lots of gas to stratovolcano.
units.task: Matching game: Students match cards describing lava properties (fluid, thick, lots of gas, few gases) to cards showing volcano shapes (shield, stratovolcano).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sequences solutions from least to most concentrated and justifies the order.
units.task: Look at the three cups of drink mix provided by the teacher. Order them from least concentrated to most concentrated. Explain how you know.

units.mastery_criterion: Student designs a logical sequence using both settling and filtering to improve water clarity.
units.task: You have a bucket of muddy water with leaves and rocks. Write a step-by-step plan using decantation and filtration to make the water look clear.

units.mastery_criterion: Student justifies the negative impact of water scarcity on specific living organisms.
units.task: Read the scenario about a region with no rain for 6 months. Predict what will happen to the local trees and birds, and justify your answer.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the cups and explains that more powder makes a darker color.
units.task: Create three solutions using 1, 2, and 4 spoons of colored drink mix. Order them by color intensity and write a sentence explaining the order.

units.mastery_criterion: Student includes both decantation and filtration in their written plan and diagram.
units.task: Work in groups to write a plan to clean a specific sample of muddy water with twigs. Draw a diagram of the two-step process.

units.mastery_criterion: Student writes logical predictions based on the biological need for water.
units.task: Read three short scenarios about different environments facing drought. Write a prediction for what will happen to the local wildlife in each.

units.mastery_criterion: Reports correctly classify reproduction methods and accurately differentiate between any tropisms or nasties described in the cases.
units.task: Students evaluate a series of case studies of unusual plants (e.g., a fern growing on a wall, a Venus flytrap) and write a report classifying their reproduction and behavioral responses.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly link symptoms to the failure of specific organs (e.g., wilting to root/stem failure or excessive transpiration).
units.task: Students complete a written performance task where they must diagnose a 'sick' plant based on symptoms (e.g., wilting, no fruits) and explain which organ system or process is failing.

units.mastery_criterion: Cites the differing growth directions and lighting conditions, then names a relevant contradictory observation such as both seedlings bending the same way despite different light directions.
units.task: Compare two teacher-provided, time-stamped image sequences: one seedling bends toward a side light over several days, while another remains upright under overhead light. Identify the evidence supporting a directional growth response and propose one observation that would weaken that explanation. The images are supplied; no waiting time is counted.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the class based on a set of 3 clues.
units.task: Play a 'Guess Who' game using vertebrate characteristics to identify the correct animal class.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully identifies 3 animals using a provided 3-step dichotomous key.
units.task: Use the provided dichotomous key to identify the animal shown in the picture (a frog).

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully identifies at least 4 out of 5 animals using the key.
units.task: Use a provided dichotomous key to identify 5 local Salvadoran animals (Torogoz, Garrobo, Masacuata, Tacuazín, Sapo) from pictures.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies 3 out of 4 plastic insects using the key.
units.task: Use a dichotomous key to identify different types of plastic insects based on observable traits.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies both animals following the key's path.
units.task: Quickly identify 2 animals using a familiar dichotomous key from a previous lesson.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately records the step numbers chosen to reach the final identification.
units.task: Work in pairs to trace the path of an animal on a dichotomous key and write down the steps taken.

units.mastery_criterion: Student produces two distinct drawings, one with a labeled nucleus and one without, accompanied by an accurate explanatory sentence.
units.task: Students draw their own models of a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell, ensuring they clearly label the nucleus in the eukaryotic drawing and write a sentence explaining the difference.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the damp, warm environment as the fastest for rotting due to moisture and temperature.
units.task: Students analyze a set of photos showing food stored in different places (a damp basement, a sunny dry windowsill, a refrigerator). They must label which environment will cause the food to rot fastest and why.

units.mastery_criterion: Student records that the salt becomes wet, demonstrating that it pulls moisture out of the 'food'.
units.task: Students use wet sponges to represent fresh food. They cover one sponge in a thick layer of salt and leave another plain. They observe and record how the salt draws moisture out of the sponge over the session.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sequences the cards and identifies the step where good bacteria create a protective environment.
units.task: Students sequence a set of cards showing the cheese-making process, focusing on the step where good bacteria are added to produce acid and protect the milk from spoiling by bad bacteria.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies the spore-growing organism as fungi and the water-hunting organism as protozoa.
units.task: Students read short descriptions of mystery microorganisms and classify them as either fungi or protozoa based on their habitat and feeding behavior.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches encurtido to acid/vinegar and dried fish to dehydration.
units.task: Students create a matching chart connecting the local food (Encurtido, Pescado seco) to the scientific principle that preserves it (Acid/Vinegar environment, Dehydration/Removal of water).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts the foods and justifies that refrigeration slows down the rotting process for perishable items.
units.task: Students sort picture cards of various foods into two categories: 'Needs Refrigeration' and 'Can Stay on Table'. They must verbally justify one choice from each category based on microbial growth speed.

units.mastery_criterion: Student demonstrates and explains that the virus model requires the cell model to simulate reproduction.
units.task: Students use clay to model a virus and a cell. They must demonstrate how the virus cannot do anything on its own until it attaches to the cell model (the host).

units.mastery_criterion: Student places 'has cells' and 'reproduces alone' in the bacterium section, and 'needs a host' in the virus section.
units.task: Students complete a Venn diagram comparing a virus and a bacterium, applying their knowledge of which traits belong to each (e.g., presence of cells, ability to reproduce independently).

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies projectile motion and mentions forward and vertical movement.
units.task: Students look at a picture of a basketball being thrown toward a hoop and describe the type of motion and the directions it is moving.

units.mastery_criterion: Student records measurements that are within +/- 0.5 cm of the actual length.
units.task: Students work in pairs to measure and record the length of 5 specific classroom objects (e.g., desk edge, book, pencil) in centimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Student draws a curved trajectory and labels the forward and vertical motions.
units.task: Students build a simple popsicle stick catapult and launch a small plastic spoon or cotton ball, observing and drawing the curved path (projectile motion).

units.mastery_criterion: Student draws equal and opposite arrows for gravity (down) and the table's push (up).
units.task: Students look at a diagram of a book resting on a table and draw arrows to represent the balanced forces acting on it.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly fills in 'friction' and 'opposes' (or similar terms).
units.task: Students complete a quick fill-in-the-blank paragraph about why a rolling ball eventually stops on grass.

units.mastery_criterion: Sketch shows lines connecting poles and clustering at the ends.
units.task: Students sketch a magnetic field from memory on a mini-whiteboard and hold it up for the teacher to check.

units.mastery_criterion: Student measures all 3 lines accurately within +/- 0.5 cm.
units.task: Students are given 3 pre-drawn lines on a paper and must quickly measure and record their lengths in centimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify melting and dissolving as physical, and rusting as chemical.
units.task: Rotate through stations observing safe changes: melting ice, dissolving sugar in water, and observing pre-rusted steel wool. Classify each change on a recording sheet.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately sort at least 8 out of 10 cards into the correct categories.
units.task: Sort picture cards of everyday scenarios (e.g., baking bread, cutting wood, rotting fruit, molding clay) into physical and chemical change categories.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify melted ice as reversible, and the broken cup and burned paper as irreversible.
units.task: Categorize images of a broken cup, melted ice, and burned paper as reversible or irreversible on a worksheet.

units.mastery_criterion: Students categorize folding as reversible and cutting as irreversible.
units.task: Students test folding a piece of paper into an origami shape versus cutting a piece of paper into pieces. They categorize each action.

units.mastery_criterion: Posters contain at least three correct examples in each column.
units.task: Create a group poster with two columns: Reversible and Irreversible. Draw or paste examples of changes in the correct columns.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly classifies colored water as homogeneous (looks uniform) and pebble water as heterogeneous (can see parts).
units.task: Observe two sealed jars provided by the teacher (one with colored water, one with water and pebbles). Write down the classification for each and explain why.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify water/salt and water/sugar as homogeneous, and water/oil and rice/beans as heterogeneous.
units.task: Students work in groups to create four safe mixtures (water/salt, water/oil, rice/beans, water/sugar) and classify them on a chart.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 80% of the photographs.
units.task: Analyze photographs of everyday items (e.g., milk, a salad, concrete, clear apple juice) and classify them as homogeneous or heterogeneous.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly classifies the shell rock as sedimentary, lava rock as igneous, and deformed rock as metamorphic.
units.task: Read descriptions of three rocks (one with shells, one from cooled lava, one deformed by heat/pressure). Classify each as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 4 out of 6 rocks based on observable features like layers, crystals, or banding.
units.task: Rock observation stations. Students use hand lenses to observe 6 different unidentified rock samples, note their features, and classify them into the three types.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match all descriptions to igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic categories.
units.task: Match written descriptions of rock formation and features (e.g., 'cooled quickly from lava', 'squished deep underground') to the correct rock type category on a large sorting mat.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully pours water leaving the majority of the sediment behind.
units.task: Given a cup of water with settled sand, carefully pour the water into an empty cup without transferring the sand.

units.mastery_criterion: Student sets up a filter and successfully passes a mixture through it, trapping solids.
units.task: Set up a funnel with cotton. Pour a mixture of water and dirt through it. Observe and record what stays in the cotton and what passes through.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 3 out of 4 tested substances.
units.task: Mix salt, sand, sugar, and soil into separate cups of water. Stir well. Write down which substances are soluble and which are insoluble.

units.mastery_criterion: Student builds a sloped channel leading to a basin and demonstrates increased flow when water is poured.
units.task: Using clay and a tray, build a model of a river flowing into a lake. Pour water to simulate rain and describe what happens to the river level.

units.mastery_criterion: Student colors exactly 97 parts for salt water and 3 parts for fresh water.
units.task: Using a 10x10 grid representing all the water on Earth, color the squares to show how much is salt water and how much is fresh water.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the stages of extraction, use, and return.
units.task: Arrange the provided cards (Extraction, Human use, Wastewater discharge) in the correct order and draw arrows between them.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully transfers mostly clear water while leaving the soil behind.
units.task: Mix soil and water in a cup. Wait 10 minutes for it to settle, then practice decanting the water into an empty cup without moving the soil.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully sets up the filter and records that solids stay in the cotton.
units.task: Set up a cotton filter in a funnel. Pour a mixture of water, leaves, and dirt through it. Observe and record the results.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies at least three of the four powders.
units.task: Test four safe household powders (sugar, flour, baking soda, coffee grounds) by mixing them in water and recording if they are soluble or insoluble.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully builds a channel that directs water into a lower basin.
units.task: In groups, build a landscape with clay on a tray, create a river channel, and test water flow with different amounts of poured water.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately colors 97 parts blue and 3 parts green for the Earth grid.
units.task: Work in pairs to color multiple 100-part grids representing different hypothetical planets, then color Earths grid.

units.mastery_criterion: Student includes all three stages in the correct order on their poster.
units.task: Create a poster showing the stages of water extraction, human use, and wastewater discharge, using drawings and labels.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts all four substances based on prior knowledge.
units.task: Sort a written list of known substances (salt, sand, sugar, soil) into two columns: Soluble and Insoluble, without testing them.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the powder as soluble based on the description.
units.task: Read a short experiment log describing a powder that disappeared when stirred into water. Identify if the powder was soluble or insoluble.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the shoot/root systems and flowers/fruits of the provided local plants.
units.task: Students analyze images of local agricultural plants, identifying their organ systems and reproductive parts, and discuss their importance.

units.mastery_criterion: Poster accurately depicts shoot/root systems and correctly describes transport/support functions.
units.task: Students create a 'Plant Profile' poster for a chosen local plant, drawing its systems, labeling organs, and writing captions explaining how the stem and roots keep it alive.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the tropism in at least 3 out of 4 clips.
units.task: Students are shown four silent video clips of plant growth and must hold up a whiteboard with the correct tropism name for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Comic strip accurately depicts roots growing down and stem growing up, with correct labels.
units.task: Students draw a comic strip showing a seed germinating underground, with roots showing gravitropism and the stem showing phototropism.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies 3 out of 4 scenarios as positive or negative taxisms.
units.task: Read 4 scenarios: a moth flying toward light, an earthworm moving away from light, a fish swimming toward food, and a cockroach hiding in the dark. Classify each movement.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies at least 5 out of 6 scenarios.
units.task: Read 6 short scenarios of animal movements and classify them as positive or negative taxisms.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately demonstrates movement toward or away from the stimulus based on the card.
units.task: Role-play taxisms based on prompt cards showing different stimuli.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 8 out of 10 specimens.
units.task: Examine models or images of invertebrates and categorize them into their major groups.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly assigns 4 out of 5 descriptions to the correct invertebrate group.
units.task: Read descriptions of invertebrates and assign them to the correct group on a worksheet.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 animals based on their skin covering.
units.task: Categorize an animal that has hair and does not lay eggs into its vertebrate group.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places at least 12 out of 15 animals in the correct class.
units.task: Create a chart categorizing 15 local Salvadoran animals (e.g., Torogoz, Garrobo, Masacuata) into the five vertebrate classes using picture cards.
